source.author: verg
source.text: corpora, per campos ferro quae fusa iacebant, redderet ac tumulo sineret succedere terrae; nullum cum victis certamen et aethere cassis; parceret hospitibus quondam socerisque vocatis.
source.text_original: corpora, per campos ferro quae fusa iacebant, / redderet ac tumulo sineret succedere terrae; / nullum cum victis certamen et aethere cassis; / parceret hospitibus quondam socerisque vocatis.
source.text_english: that he would restore the bodies that had been spread out on the fields by the sword and allow them to pass beneath the earth to burial mound; that he would wage no contest with the vanquished and with those fallen from the sky; that he would spare guests once invited and fathers-in-law.

reuse.author: hier
reuse.text: Quia in superiori capitulo fuerat praelocutus, quod postquam mortui fuerint homines, a corde viventium excidant, et nec dilectionem quis in eos habeat nec odium, secundum illud poetae: Nullum cum victis certamen et aethere cassis: et quia sub sole ultra nihil possint: nunc quasi errorem humanum et consuetudinem, qua se ad fruenda hujus saeculi bona invicem hortantur, inducit, et prosopopaeian facit more rhetorum et poetarum, dicens: O homo, quia ergo post mortem nihil es, et mors ipsa nihil est, audi consilium meum, et dum vivis in hac brevi vita, fruere voluptate, utere dapibus, vino curas opprime, et intellige, quoniam a Deo tibi donata sunt ad utendum.
reuse.text_original: Quia in superiori capitulo fuerat praelocutus, quod postquam mortui fuerint homines, a corde viventium excidant, et nec dilectionem quis in eos habeat nec odium, secundum illud poetae: Nullum cum victis certamen et aethere cassis: et quia sub sole ultra nihil possint: nunc quasi errorem humanum et consuetudinem, qua se ad fruenda hujus saeculi bona invicem hortantur, inducit, et προσωποποιΐαν ( prosopopaeian ) facit more rhetorum et poetarum, dicens: O homo, quia ergo post mortem nihil es, et mors ipsa nihil est, audi consilium meum, et dum vivis in hac brevi vita, fruere voluptate, utere dapibus, vino curas opprime, et intellige, quoniam a Deo tibi donata sunt ad utendum.
reuse.text_english: Because in the preceding chapter he had previously said that after men have died, they fall away from the hearts of the living, and no one has either love for them or hatred, according to that line of the poet: There is no contest with the conquered or with those whose dust is strewn to the sky; and because beyond the sun they can do nothing more: now he introduces, as it were, human error and the custom by which people urge one another to enjoy the goods of this world, and he makes a personification in the manner of rhetoricians and poets, saying: O man, since after death you are nothing, and death itself is nothing, hear my advice, and while you live in this brief life, enjoy pleasure, make use of feasts, crush cares with wine, and understand that these things have been given to you by God for your use.
